newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands ready for flood evacuation in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Thousands ready for flood evacuation in Germany.

text.p: Thousands of people in east Germany were braced for evacuation on Monday, as a fresh wave of high water rolled down the Oder River on the Polish border toward the fertile Oderbruch basin.
Local officials have warned the entire population of the region to be prepared to leave their homes at a moment's notice.

Nearly 5,000 people were evacuated from the most endangered area near the village of Hohenwutzen at the north end of the Oderbruch basin on Friday, and 9,000 were "sitting on their suitcases" in some 24 villages targeted for evacuation.
There are a total of some 19,000 residents in the region.

Officials breathed a sigh of relief that no new breaks in the dike along the Oder river were reported overnight, but said the situation remained critical. The 250-year-old dike has held back record floods for nearly two weeks.

"Under this strain the dikes are like pudding," a spokesman for the interior ministry of Brandenburg state said. "We cannot predict whether the dike will hold. We can only keep hoping and carry more sandbags."

Around 700 German soldiers and rescue workers kept vigil throughout the night, reinforcing the dike as a new flood wave that sent water levels to record highs in Frankfurt an der Oder and Slubice in neighbouring Poland approached Hohenwutzen.
Floods were now receding in Frankfurt and Slubice, officials said, but the crest of the wave was expected to pass Hohenwutzen by midday on Monday.
"The next few hours will be the toughest test so far," said an official on the flood crisis committee.

Some of central Europe's worst floods this century have claimed over 100 lives in Poland and the Czech Republic this month. Germany has escaped the worst of the crisis, but damage to homes and crops has been extensive.
Floods in Frankfurt Oder peaked at 6.57 metres (21.54 Feet) on Sunday, well above the 1930 record level of 6.35 metres (20.82 Feet).
Seven years after unification, officials say flood damage could destroy many east Germans financially, just as they are starting to get on their feet.

The worst damage threatens the Oderbruch plateau north of Frankfurt an der Oder -- a vast plain some 50 km (30 miles) long and 17 km (11 miles) wide that was created 250 years ago by Frederick the Great, who drained the moors and redirected the flow of the river Oder to create the fertile basin for farmland.

Because the area is considerably lower than the river itself, any serious break in the 70-km section of dike protecting the Oderbruch would flood the entire region in a matter of hours, submerging some 17 villages and ruining crops.
Large sections of the dike have collapsed over the past few days, and a 30-km section between Kienitz in the south and Hohenwutzen is particularly threatened.

The highest water levels in Oderbruch were registered in 1940, when measuring stations in Hohensaaten, near Hohenwutzen, reported 7.78 metres, (25.51 Feet) compared to 6.94 now. In Kienitz water levels were at 6.10 metres, near the 1940 level of 6.30.
Further south, there have been three breaks in the dike over the past few days, flooding towns.
The worst hit areas in Germany were Brieskow-Finkenheerd, Wiesenau and Ziltendorf, where the Oder overflowed its banks, rising to the tops of houses in villages some five km (three miles) away.
